claims.text: HEA coating wear performance is primarily governed by in-situ formation of a continuous, mechanically robust oxide layer.
The oxide layer acts as a self-lubricating barrier against abrasive and adhesive wear.
Oxidizing environments cause an oxide film to form uniformly on a homogeneous HEA coating.
A uniform oxide film distributes contact stresses and reduces direct metal contact during friction.
The baseline material is a homogeneous AlCoCrFeNi-based HEA coating with minimal pre-existing oxide and a uniform microstructure.
Ambient air will promote oxide formation relative to argon or vacuum.
Argon or vacuum will suppress oxide formation during wear testing.
The proposed comparison applies from room temperature to 800 °C.
The structural mediator is a well-adhered, uniformly distributed ultra-nanocrystalline or lamellar oxide film on the wear track.
The oxide film lowers friction and wear by redistributing contact stresses and reducing metal-to-metal asperity contact.
No comparable protective film develops under inert conditions.
Oxidizing conditions will produce lower friction coefficients than inert conditions.
Oxidizing conditions will produce lower wear rates than inert conditions.
Wear improvement will saturate beyond an oxygen-availability threshold.
The proposed mechanism is limited to coatings with homogeneous microstructures and phase compositions at temperatures up to 800 °C.
Significant defects, large phase separations, or an excessively thick or brittle oxide scale can invalidate the mechanism.
Comparable wear rates, friction coefficients, and surface characteristics in inert and oxidizing tests, despite the absence of a protective oxide in the inert test, would falsify the hypothesis.
